sourcesRead.title: GM Don't List #13: Boxed Text Pitfalls (Justin Alexander, The Alexandrian)
Dungeon Mastering 101: Mastering the Boxed Text (Dungeon Master's Workshop)
Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1 (Jesse Decker and David Noonan, Wizards of the Coast)
Retrospective: The Village of Hommlet (James Maliszewski, Grognardia)
A different kind of naturalism (Jim Nelson)
Thinking Outside the Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, Critical Hits)
Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text (Shawn Merwin, D&D Beyond)
How much description should a dungeon key include? (David Hartlage, DMDavid)

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch lists boxed text among the things he does not want in an adventure module.
claims.quote: Boxed text is usually not a good thing.

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch names a terse writing style as one of the things he looks for in an adventure module.
claims.quote: Terse writing style

claims.claim: Bryce Lynch says in a comment on his own standards page that he loathes overly long backstory and fiction introductions in modules.
claims.source: Bryce Lynch, comment of 19 April 2016 on 'Review Standards', tenfootpole.org
claims.quote: I LOATHE the overly long backstory

claims.claim: The tenfootpole reviewer who writes as 'The Pretty Girl' puts succinct-and-evocative at the top of her four-point Language scale for modules; the scale is hers, not Bryce Lynch's.
claims.source: 'The Pretty Girl', rating scale on 'Review Standards', tenfootpole.org
claims.quote: 4 – Succinct and evocative
claims.page: Review Standards, 'The Pretty Girl' section, Language scale

claims.claim: Justin Alexander defines boxed text in an RPG scenario as narration written in advance for the GM to read to the players.
claims.quote: a prewritten narration designed to be read to the players

claims.claim: Justin Alexander names the reaction point and says a description must not carry the world past it before the players may respond; he applies the test to a boxed passage he quotes from Journeys Through the Radiant Citadel.
claims.quote: the game world continue to move forward past the reaction point

claims.claim: A commenter on Alexander's post recalls a lost Wizards devblog article arguing GM-delivered descriptive text should stop at three sentences; the recollection is the commenter's, and the original article is not linked.
claims.source: commenter 'mellonbread', comment of 2 August 2022 on The Alexandrian
claims.quote: should never be longer than three sentences
claims.confidence: medium — a reader's memory of an article he says was deleted; unverified against the original

claims.claim: David Noonan reports that from watching games at Gen Con 2005 he concluded a DM reading boxed text holds player attention for two sentences.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, 'Design & Development: Undercover at Gen Con, Part 1', Wizards of the Coast
claims.quote: If you’re the DM, you get two sentences. Period.

claims.claim: Noonan's stated mechanism for the attention loss is that read-aloud text converts the game's normal conversation into oration.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, Wizards of the Coast
claims.quote: Boxed text replaces that conversation with oration.

claims.claim: Noonan sets a three-sentence 2005 boxed text from Sons of Gruumsh beside a much longer one from 1999's Return to the Keep on the Borderlands to show that read-aloud text used to be far longer.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, Wizards of the Coast
claims.quote: Boxed text in adventures used to be a lot longer

claims.claim: Noonan reports that players who heard boxed text still missed its factual content, naming room dimensions, exits and monster counts as what went past them.
claims.source: Jesse Decker and David Noonan, Wizards of the Coast
claims.quote: basic stuff, like room dimensions, how many doors exit the room

claims.claim: The Dungeon Master's Workshop close reading of King Bruenor's speech in Out of the Abyss objects that the passage is formatted like a novel, with a 'he says' attribution tag inside text meant to be spoken.
claims.source: Dungeon Master's Workshop, 'Dungeon Mastering 101: Mastering the Boxed Text'
claims.quote: structuring the narrative like it’s a book
claims.page: section on Out of the Abyss

claims.claim: The same close reading notes that Out of the Abyss's own instruction immediately after the Bruenor boxed text tells the DM to paraphrase it.
claims.source: Dungeon Master's Workshop, quoting Out of the Abyss
claims.quote: Paraphrase Bruenor’s speech as needed
claims.page: section on Out of the Abyss

claims.claim: Dungeon Master's Workshop advises that a boxed text containing a paragraph break is usually already twice as long as it should be.
claims.quote: already too long by half

claims.claim: Dungeon Master's Workshop offers third-person objective and second-person subjective as two switchable registers for the same location description, illustrating each with a waterfall sentence.
claims.quote: A 200-foot waterfall cascades down

claims.claim: Dungeon Master's Workshop reports that Waterdeep: Dragon Heist describes minor locations in mixed forms, a bookstore getting a short paraphrasable paragraph and a villa's great hall a set of bullet points.
claims.quote: A bookstore receives a short paragraph description

claims.claim: James Maliszewski praises the names of Hommlet's inhabitants as Gygax at his best and lists five of them.
claims.quote: are Gygax at his mellifluent best

claims.claim: Maliszewski singles out the holy sayings of St Cuthbert printed in The Village of Hommlet and quotes three of them in capitals as they appear in the module.
claims.quote: his holy sayings presented in the module

claims.claim: Jim Nelson reads Hommlet's villager entries as an iceberg: their ambitions, suspicions and secrets enrich the setting although the players will probably never meet them.
claims.source: Jim Nelson, novelist, 'A different kind of naturalism'
claims.quote: make the setting richer even if little of it is presented

claims.claim: Nelson cites a Hommlet household entry's exact hidden sum as the kind of specific detail that implies a story behind it.
claims.source: Jim Nelson, 'A different kind of naturalism'
claims.quote: stashed seventy-three silver coins in the hollow of a tree

claims.claim: Nelson quotes a reviewer's line that Hommlet is a place whose history shapes its layout, mood and inhabitants.
claims.source: Jim Nelson quoting an unnamed reviewer
claims.quote: is a place with history and its history shapes and affects
claims.confidence: medium — Nelson attributes the sentence only to 'one reviewer' and gives no link

claims.claim: Shawn Merwin's first rule for boxed text is to move from second person to third, and he supplies the same clearing in both, the third-person version making the corpse the subject.
claims.quote: The bloated corpse of a headless dragon dominates the center

claims.claim: Merwin's rule of thumb as a writer and editor is to keep only the environmental details the characters will have to interact with.
claims.quote: leave in only the details about the environment

claims.claim: Merwin's own model opening boxed text, printed in the article, is four sentences and under a hundred words, and he then explains what each of the four sentences does.
claims.source: Shawn Merwin, 'Let's Design an Adventure: Boxed Text', D&D Beyond
claims.quote: Four sentences, and less than 100 words.

claims.claim: Merwin tells adventure writers to avoid 'seems to be' and 'appears to be' in read-aloud text because for the characters perception is reality and the hedge invites metagaming.
claims.quote: For the characters, perception is reality.

claims.claim: Merwin makes reading boxed text aloud a required check, naming tongue-twisters and unintended alliteration as faults invisible on the page.
claims.quote: funny-sounding phrases, unintended alliteration

claims.claim: Merwin tells writers not to use game-mechanical words such as stunned or frightened in their ordinary sense inside read-aloud text.
claims.quote: Avoid game mechanical terms used in a non-mechanical way

claims.claim: Merwin says writing good boxed text needs the precision of fiction or poetry while also doing the work of technical writing.
claims.quote: the same precision that one might use for fiction or poetry

claims.claim: David Hartlage reads the 1989 Gamescience expansion of a Tegel Manor bedroom key as one good middle sentence padded out to length.
claims.quote: pads it like a school paper stretched to an assigned length

claims.claim: Hartlage attributes the padding to the format itself: the custom of long descriptions makes authors write even where they have nothing to add.
claims.quote: encourages authors to write something even when they have little to add

claims.claim: Hartlage argues a location's description should be sized to its purpose in play, instancing a sheriff met about a wanted poster whose kitchen needs no inventory.
claims.quote: no one needs an item-by-item inventory of her kitchen
claims.page: Matching description to a location's purpose

claims.claim: Hartlage says Curse of Strahd gives pages of room description to notable NPCs' homes and calls Chris Perkins's details creepy and moody while judging most of those rooms unreachable in play.
claims.quote: The homes of notable NPCs get pages of room descriptions.
claims.page: Matching description to a location's purpose

claims.claim: Hartlage reports that Curse of Strahd carries boxed text for every location while its successor Storm King's Thunder omits almost all read-aloud text.
claims.quote: omits almost all read-aloud text
